done.why: The world told me I'd used all 250 turns. I was standing in the Mirror Room with a trunk of jewels I never got home, just after touching the mirror made the earth rumble.

about: It's the white house and the Great Underground Empire again, but altered. You loot treasures from under the house and bring them back to the trophy case, past a troll, a thief who will kill you, a maze, a dam and a mirror. The changes I noticed were mostly about weight and what you're allowed to carry. The chimney fits you, your lamp and one more thing. Your load fills up fast, and the sword is "not least of it". When you die, the world puts your things back in a tidy order. Plain things end up scattered in the forest, valuables roll somewhere under the house, and someone puts the lamp back in the living room.

moments.note: I typed 'roll up the rug and wear it'. It moved the rug and showed the trap door, then choked on the 'wear it' half. Half a contrary sentence worked.
Giving the troll my lunch worked: he 'graciously accepts the gift'. Later he ate my garlic too, but he kept fighting anyway.
The gothic lettering reads 'This space intentionally left blank.'
The maze cost me about 50 turns. On repeat visits rooms often showed just 'Maze' with no description, so I couldn't tell them apart.
I found the Grating Room, and the skeleton key from the dead adventurer opened it to the clearing. That was a satisfying shortcut.
The painting has a new, tender description: a sunlit valley that is 'hard to look at for long, and harder to look away'.
The chimney refused me and listed everything I carried. It has room for 'you, your lamp and one thing more'. It was a clear, fair rule, and I solved it by dropping everything but the painting.
I handed the thief my skeleton key on a whim and he 'thanks you politely'. Pure contrary fun.

I picked a fight with the thief and died in three rounds. I had typed several lines ahead without reading, so the death caught me by surprise and those queued moves were wasted wandering the forest empty-handed.

The death text explains where things went: plain things in the fields, valuables in a dark corner, and the lamp put back by 'somebody tidy'. When I returned to the living room, the lamp really was there.
I never found the platinum bar again. 'Rolled into some dark corner' didn't tell me which one.
'Your load is too heavy, the sword not least of it' kept stopping me from taking the pump and the trident, even after I dropped the wrench.
Touching the mirror made the earth rumble and the room shake. Then my turns ran out.

wished: Say compound or odd sentences ('put the leaflet back and eat the mailbox', 'swim anyway', 'sign the painting with the paint') and get something other than 'That sentence isn't one I recognize'.
Read the leaflet without taking it. The game took it for me anyway.
Pry the nails out of the gothic door with the sword.
Climb the 'unclimbable' ramp, or at least get a reply that wasn't just a parser refusal.
Get more help finding the platinum bar after death, since the respawn text said valuables rolled into a dark corner.
Have time to find out what the mirror's rumble did and to get the trunk and trident home.

lines.line: The engravings translate to "This space intentionally left blank."
lines.why: A dry joke on a door that won't open. It felt like the world winking back at me.

lines.line: It is a painting of a sunlit valley, done with such tenderness that it is hard to look at it for long, and harder to look away.
lines.why: The most beautiful line I read. It made stealing the painting feel like something.

lines.line: The chimney has room for you, your lamp and one thing more, and not an inch besides.
lines.why: It turned a refusal into a puzzle with a clear rule.

lines.line: The thief places the skeleton key in his bag and thanks you politely.
lines.why: It rewarded a silly contrary move with manners.

lines.line: The plain things are strewn about the forest and the fields around the house, anything of value has rolled into some dark corner in or under it, and somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.
lines.why: Death that sorts your belongings for you. Strange and kind of sweet, and it was true: the lamp was waiting.

lines.line: Your load is too heavy, the sword not least of it.
lines.why: I read it so often it became the voice of the game, a nagging hint to put the sword down.

fun.why: The troll fight, opening the grate, the chimney rule and handing the thief my key were fun. The maze slog and my careless death against the thief took a lot of the fun away.

engagement.why: I kept wanting to see the next room. The dam and draining the reservoir pulled me along, and the mirror rumble left me wanting more just as my turns ran out.

difficulty.why: The maze ate dozens of turns because its rooms barely describe themselves. The weight limit blocked me again and again. The thief killed me in three rounds. With a 250-turn budget it felt punishing.

interestingness.why: I liked the changes to the familiar world: the chimney's carrying rule, the death that tidies your things, the painting's new description, and the polite thief. They made me pay attention instead of coasting on memory.

prose.why: The new lines are better than the old ones: the painting, the chimney, the tidy death. The parser's flat 'That sentence isn't one I recognize' broke the spell every time I phrased something oddly.
